title: BPP versus BQP
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.

importance.reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.

progress.text: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with the containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\); the inspected 2019 book states it as Theorem 11.2.
Shor’s polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms give major candidate advantages without an unconditional classical lower bound.
Boykin and coauthors prove universality of the finite Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT basis used here.
Raz–Tal establish a separation from the polynomial hierarchy relative to an oracle, preserving that oracle restriction.
Quantum publishes the shallow-circuit sampling separation, with explicit classical randomness/fan-in restrictions and a different output task.
A new oracle separates the promise-class comparison from the total-language comparison even when the language classes coincide.

status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.

context_blocks.text: Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes on this card still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

sentences: BPP and BQP are classes of total decision languages with bounded error separately on every input, using classical randomness and quantum circuits respectively.
The quantum model uses one polynomial-time classical generator for finite H, T and CNOT circuits with auxiliary qubits initialized to zero and one final measured bit.
The question asks whether some quantum polynomial-time language has no classical randomized polynomial-time decider; the alternative is equality of the classes.
Factoring algorithms, oracle separations and shallow sampling lower bounds retain assumptions or output/resource differences that do not establish this full separation.
A September 2026 oracle result further distinguishes total-language equality from promise-class equality, while the ordinary total-language target remains unresolved in the inspected sources.

The card keeps its finite H, T, CNOT basis and now gives explicit matrices, uniformity and measurement semantics.
